examName: IRS Enrolled Agent Special Enrollment Examination (SEE)
tagline: Prepare for all three parts of the IRS Enrolled Agent exam.

domains.name: Part 1: Individuals
domains.description: Individual taxpayer data, income, deductions, credits, and specialized returns.

domains.name: Part 2: Businesses
domains.description: Business entities, business tax preparation, and specialized business returns.

domains.name: Part 3A: Representation before the IRS
domains.description: Authority to represent taxpayers and specific areas of representation before the IRS.

domains.name: Part 3B: Practices, Procedures and Filing
domains.description: Practitioner rules under Circular 230, the Office of Professional Responsibility, and the filing process.

questions.stem: Maria is unmarried, paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for the year, and her 12-year-old son lived with her for the entire year. No one else can claim either of them. Which filing status is most advantageous and available to Maria?

options.text: Single
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing separately

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Head of household applies to an unmarried (or considered-unmarried) taxpayer who pays more than half the cost of keeping up a home that is the main home of a qualifying person, such as a dependent child, for more than half the year; it gives a larger standard deduction and wider brackets than single. Why the others are wrong: **A** single is available but less favorable than head of household when she qualifies; **C** qualifying surviving spouse requires a spouse who died in one of the two prior years, which is not stated; **D** married filing separately requires being married.

questions.stem: To be claimed as a qualifying child, an individual generally must meet an age test. Apart from being permanently and totally disabled, which statement correctly describes the age test?

options.text: Under age 17 at year-end with no exception for students
Under age 19 with no exception for students of any age
Under age 19 at year-end, or under age 24 if a full-time student for at least five months, and younger than the taxpayer
Any age, because there is no age test for a qualifying child

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A qualifying child must be under 19 at the end of the year, or under 24 if a full-time student for at least five months of the year, and must be younger than the taxpayer (the age test is waived only if the child is permanently and totally disabled). Why the others are wrong: **A** under 17 is the age limit for the child tax credit, not the qualifying-child age test; **B** ignores the full-time-student exception that extends the limit to under 24; **D** a qualifying child does have an age test, unlike a qualifying relative.

questions.stem: An employee receives a $5,000 distribution of qualified scholarship funds used to pay tuition and required course fees at an accredited college where she is a degree candidate. How is the scholarship treated for federal income tax?

options.text: Fully taxable as wages because it was paid to the student
Tax-free, because amounts used for tuition and required fees by a degree candidate are excluded from gross income
Tax-free only if the student is pursuing a graduate degree
Always taxable because scholarships are never excludable

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A scholarship is tax-free to a degree candidate to the extent it is used for qualified education expenses—tuition and fees required for enrollment plus required books, supplies, and equipment. Why the others are wrong: **A** a qualified scholarship for tuition is not treated as wages unless it represents payment for required services; **C** the exclusion applies to undergraduate and graduate degree candidates alike; **D** amounts spent on room and board are taxable, but qualified tuition amounts are excludable, so 'always taxable' is wrong.

questions.stem: Devon sold 100 shares of stock he had held for eight months at a $4,000 gain and 100 shares of a different stock held for three years at a $1,000 loss. He has no other capital transactions. How is the net result taxed for the year?

options.text: A $3,000 net short-term capital gain taxed at ordinary rates
A $3,000 net long-term capital gain taxed at preferential rates
A $4,000 short-term gain and a separate $1,000 long-term loss that cannot offset it
A $3,000 ordinary loss

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Long-term losses first net against long-term gains and short-term losses against short-term gains; here the $1,000 long-term loss has no long-term gain, so it nets against the $4,000 short-term gain, leaving a $3,000 net short-term gain taxed as ordinary income. Why the others are wrong: **B** the surviving net gain is short-term, not long-term, so it does not get preferential rates; **C** short- and long-term results are netted against each other after netting within each class; **D** the result is a net gain, not a loss.

questions.stem: A single taxpayer sold her main home in 2025 for a $200,000 gain. She owned and used it as her principal residence for the prior six years and has not excluded gain on another home sale in the past two years. How much gain may she exclude?

options.text: $0; gain on a personal residence is never excludable
The entire $200,000, because a single taxpayer may exclude up to $250,000 of gain
$100,000, because only half of any residence gain is excludable
The entire $200,000, but only because she is over age 55

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the Section 121 exclusion, a single taxpayer who owned and used the home as a principal residence for at least two of the last five years may exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 if married filing jointly and both tests are met), so her $200,000 gain is fully excluded. Why the others are wrong: **A** residence gain is excludable when the ownership and use tests are met; **C** there is no general 'half the gain' rule; **D** the old age-55 one-time exclusion was repealed—age is irrelevant to Section 121.

questions.stem: Grace, age 45, took a $10,000 distribution from her traditional IRA to pay credit-card debt. The entire IRA was funded with deductible contributions and no exception applies. What is the federal tax consequence?

options.text: The distribution is tax-free because IRA withdrawals are always nontaxable
Only the 10% additional tax applies; the $10,000 is not included in income
$10,000 is included in income and a 10% additional tax of $1,000 applies
The distribution is subject to a 20% additional tax for early withdrawal

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A distribution from a fully deductible traditional IRA is included in gross income, and because Grace is under 59½ with no applicable exception, a 10% additional tax applies on top of the regular income tax—$1,000 on the $10,000. Why the others are wrong: **A** distributions of pre-tax IRA funds are taxable; **B** the amount is also includible in income, not just subject to the penalty; **D** the early-distribution additional tax is 10%, not 20%.

questions.stem: For tax year 2025, a married-filing-jointly couple has $30,000 of itemizable expenses, while the standard deduction for their status is $31,500. Setting aside any limitations, what should they generally do?

options.text: Take the standard deduction, because it exceeds their itemized deductions
Itemize, because itemizing is always better than the standard deduction
Take both the standard deduction and itemized deductions
Take neither; deductions are optional and reduce refunds

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A taxpayer chooses the greater of the standard deduction or total allowable itemized deductions; since the $31,500 standard deduction exceeds their $30,000 of itemized deductions, taking the standard deduction yields the lower taxable income. Why the others are wrong: **B** itemizing only helps when itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction, which is not the case here; **C** a taxpayer cannot claim both the standard deduction and itemized deductions; **D** deductions reduce taxable income and are beneficial, so taking neither is wrong.

questions.stem: A taxpayer paid $14,000 of qualified residence mortgage interest, $9,000 of state and local taxes (income and property), and made $5,000 of cash charitable gifts to public charities. For 2025, which limitation most directly affects these itemized deductions?

options.text: The state and local tax deduction is capped at $40,000 ($20,000 if married filing separately)
Mortgage interest is capped at $10,000 per year
Cash charitable gifts to public charities are nondeductible
All itemized deductions are limited to 2% of adjusted gross income

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** For 2025 the deduction for combined state and local income (or sales) and property taxes is limited to $40,000 ($20,000 for married filing separately); here the $9,000 is fully deductible but the SALT cap is the relevant limitation. Why the others are wrong: **B** mortgage interest is limited by acquisition-debt principal (generally $750,000), not a flat $10,000 of interest; **C** cash gifts to public charities are deductible, generally up to 60% of AGI; **D** the 2%-of-AGI floor applied to miscellaneous itemized deductions, which are currently suspended, not to all itemized deductions.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the child tax credit for a qualifying child for tax year 2025 (ignoring income phase-outs)?

options.text: A fully refundable $3,000 credit for any dependent of any age
A nonrefundable $500 credit for each qualifying child under age 17
A deduction of $2,200 from adjusted gross income per child
Up to $2,200 per qualifying child under age 17, with a portion refundable as the additional child tax credit

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** For 2025 the child tax credit is up to $2,200 per qualifying child under age 17 (who has an SSN), and up to $1,700 is refundable as the additional child tax credit. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is not fully refundable and the child must generally be under 17; **B** the $500 credit for other dependents is the credit for dependents who are not qualifying children, not the child tax credit; **C** it is a credit against tax, not a deduction from AGI.

questions.stem: A self-employed consultant pays $9,000 in self-employment tax for the year. How does this affect the federal income tax return?

options.text: The full self-employment tax is deductible as an itemized deduction
Self-employment tax is not deductible in any form
One-half of the self-employment tax is deductible as an adjustment to income (above the line)
The full self-employment tax is a credit against income tax

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A taxpayer may deduct one-half of self-employment tax as an adjustment to gross income (above the line), which approximates the employer-equivalent share of FICA. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is an above-the-line adjustment, not an itemized deduction, and only half is deductible; **B** half is deductible, so 'not deductible at all' is wrong; **D** it reduces taxable income as a deduction, not as a dollar-for-dollar credit.

questions.stem: A taxpayer receives $20,000 of Social Security benefits and has substantial other income. Which statement about the federal taxation of Social Security benefits is correct?

options.text: Social Security benefits are always fully tax-free
100% of benefits are always included in gross income
Benefits are taxable only for taxpayers under full retirement age
Up to 85% of benefits may be included in gross income depending on the taxpayer's combined income

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Depending on provisional (combined) income, 0%, up to 50%, or up to 85% of Social Security benefits are includible in gross income; higher income pushes more of the benefit into taxable income. Why the others are wrong: **A** benefits are not always tax-free; **B** at most 85% is taxable, never the full 100%; **C** taxability depends on income, not on whether the recipient has reached full retirement age.

questions.stem: An individual taxpayer expects to owe $6,000 in tax this year after withholding. To avoid an underpayment penalty under the general safe harbors (AGI not over $150,000), what is the minimum the taxpayer must have paid in through withholding and timely estimates?

options.text: The smaller of 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's tax
Exactly 100% of the current year's tax, with no other option
At least 50% of the current year's tax
Nothing, because individuals are never subject to an underpayment penalty

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The estimated-tax safe harbor is met by paying the smaller of 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000), avoiding the underpayment penalty. Why the others are wrong: **B** 90% of the current year or the prior-year figure also works, so 100% of the current year is not the only option; **C** 50% is below the required threshold; **D** individuals can owe an underpayment penalty when withholding and estimates fall short.

questions.stem: A taxpayer asks an enrolled agent how long to keep records that support items on a filed federal income tax return when no fraud is involved and all income was reported. Which guideline is generally appropriate?

options.text: Keep supporting records generally until the period of limitations for that return expires, typically at least three years from filing
Records must be destroyed immediately after the return is filed
Records only need to be kept for 30 days after filing
There is no reason to keep any records once a refund is received

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Records that support income, deductions, and credits should generally be kept until the period of limitations for that return runs out—usually at least three years from the date the return was filed (longer in some situations, such as unreported income or worthless-security/bad-debt claims). Why the others are wrong: **B** destroying records immediately leaves nothing to substantiate the return if examined; **C** 30 days is far shorter than the assessment period; **D** receiving a refund does not end the IRS's ability to examine the return within the limitations period.

questions.stem: Which two amounts are generally excluded from a taxpayer's gross income for federal income tax purposes? (Select two.)

options.text: Interest received on a State of Ohio municipal bond
Compensatory damages received on account of a physical personal injury
Unemployment compensation
Gambling winnings

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Interest on state and local municipal bonds is excluded from federal gross income, and damages received on account of personal physical injuries or sickness are also excludable under Section 104. Why the others are wrong: **C** unemployment compensation is fully includible in gross income; **D** gambling winnings are taxable income (losses are deductible only to the extent of winnings if the taxpayer itemizes).

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to claim the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC) for a dependent. Which two conditions must be satisfied? (Select two.)

options.text: The student must be pursuing a degree or recognized credential and enrolled at least half-time for at least one academic period
The credit may be claimed for an unlimited number of tax years for the same student
The student must not have completed the first four years of postsecondary education before the year begins
The student must be enrolled in graduate-level coursework only

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** The AOTC requires the student to be pursuing a degree or credential, enrolled at least half-time for at least one academic period, and to be within the first four years of postsecondary education (not yet completed before the year). Why the others are wrong: **B** the AOTC is limited to four tax years per eligible student; **D** the AOTC applies to undergraduate-level study, whereas the Lifetime Learning Credit covers graduate work.

questions.stem: Place the following components in the correct order as they appear in the individual income tax computation, from earliest to latest.

options.text: Total (gross) income
Adjusted gross income (AGI)
Taxable income
Tax liability before credits

questions.explanation: The individual tax formula proceeds in this sequence: first sum all includible items into total (gross) income (A); subtract above-the-line adjustments to reach adjusted gross income (B); subtract the greater of the standard or itemized deduction (and any QBI deduction) to reach taxable income (C); then apply the rate schedule to taxable income to determine the tax liability before credits (D). Following this order is essential because each figure is the starting point for the next, and credits and other taxes are applied only after the tax before credits is computed.

questions.stem: Two individuals start a business together, share profits and losses, and file an information return reporting the entity's income, but the entity itself pays no federal income tax. Each owner reports a distributive share on their own return. What type of entity is this most likely to be?

options.text: A C corporation
A general partnership
A sole proprietorship
A tax-exempt organization

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A partnership is a pass-through entity that files an information return (Form 1065) but pays no entity-level federal income tax; each partner reports a distributive share of income, deductions, and credits via Schedule K-1. Why the others are wrong: **A** a C corporation pays entity-level tax; **C** a sole proprietorship has only one owner; **D** a tax-exempt organization is not a for-profit business shared by owners reporting distributive shares.

questions.stem: A profitable C corporation distributes a $50,000 cash dividend to its sole shareholder out of current earnings and profits. Which statement best describes the federal tax treatment?

options.text: The corporation deducts the dividend, and the shareholder excludes it
The corporation cannot deduct the dividend, and the shareholder includes it in income (double taxation)
Neither the corporation nor the shareholder has any tax consequence
The shareholder deducts the dividend as a business expense

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A C corporation cannot deduct dividends paid, and a dividend out of earnings and profits is taxable to the shareholder—the classic 'double taxation' of corporate earnings. Why the others are wrong: **A** dividends are not deductible by the payer and are generally taxable to the recipient; **C** there is a tax consequence to the shareholder; **D** a shareholder does not deduct dividends received—they are income, not an expense.

questions.stem: An S corporation has a single shareholder who materially participates in the business. The corporation earns $80,000 of ordinary business income. How is this income generally taxed?

options.text: The S corporation pays corporate income tax on the $80,000
The income passes through and is taxed on the shareholder's individual return, whether or not distributed
The income is tax-free until actually distributed to the shareholder
The income is subject to self-employment tax on the shareholder's full distributive share

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An S corporation is a pass-through entity; its ordinary income flows through on Schedule K-1 and is taxed to the shareholder in the year earned, regardless of whether it is distributed. Why the others are wrong: **A** an S corporation generally pays no federal income tax at the entity level; **C** pass-through income is taxed when earned, not when distributed; **D** an S corporation shareholder's distributive share is not subject to self-employment tax (though a shareholder-employee must take reasonable W-2 wages).

questions.stem: A partner contributes equipment with a $30,000 fair market value and a $12,000 adjusted basis to a partnership in exchange for a partnership interest, in a transaction qualifying under Section 721. What is the partner's basis in the partnership interest from this contribution, ignoring liabilities?

options.text: $30,000, the fair market value of the equipment
$12,000, a carryover of the partner's adjusted basis in the equipment
$0, because contributions are taxable events
$18,000, the built-in gain on the equipment

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under Section 721 no gain or loss is recognized on a contribution of property to a partnership in exchange for an interest, and the partner's outside basis is a carryover (substituted) basis equal to the property's adjusted basis—$12,000. Why the others are wrong: **A** fair market value is not used; basis carries over; **C** the contribution is generally nontaxable, so basis is not zero; **D** the $18,000 built-in gain is preserved but is not the partner's basis.

questions.stem: A cash-method sole proprietor receives a check from a client on December 30, 2025, but does not deposit it until January 5, 2026. When is the income recognized?

options.text: In 2025, when the check was received and available without restriction
In 2026, when the check was deposited
Half in 2025 and half in 2026
Only when the bank reports the interest to the IRS

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the cash method and the doctrine of constructive receipt, income is recognized when it is received or made available without substantial restriction; receiving the check on December 30, 2025 fixes recognition in 2025 even if deposited later. Why the others are wrong: **B** deferral until deposit ignores constructive receipt; **C** there is no splitting of a single payment; **D** recognition does not depend on bank reporting of interest, which is unrelated to the fee income.

questions.stem: A business places a piece of qualifying tangible personal property in service. Which depreciation system is generally used for federal income tax purposes for such property placed in service today?

options.text: Straight-line depreciation over the asset's entire economic life with no conventions
The units-of-production method required by the IRS
The Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS)
Immediate full expensing is mandatory for all assets

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** MACRS is the cost-recovery system used for most tangible business property placed in service after 1986, assigning recovery periods and conventions (e.g., half-year or mid-quarter) by asset class. Why the others are wrong: **A** tax depreciation uses prescribed recovery periods and conventions, not the asset's full economic life; **B** units-of-production is not the required federal tax method; **D** Section 179 expensing and bonus depreciation are elective or limited, not a mandatory full write-off for every asset.

questions.stem: A business sells equipment it had depreciated, recognizing a gain. Part of the gain equals the depreciation previously taken. Under Section 1245, how is that portion of the gain characterized?

options.text: Ordinary income to the extent of depreciation recapture
Long-term capital gain regardless of depreciation taken
Tax-free return of capital
A deductible business loss

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Section 1245 recaptures gain on the disposition of depreciable personal property as ordinary income up to the amount of depreciation previously claimed; any gain beyond that may be Section 1231 gain. Why the others are wrong: **B** the recapture portion is ordinary, not capital; **C** recognized gain is not a tax-free return of capital; **D** the transaction produces a gain, not a loss.

questions.stem: A business incurs $5,000 entertaining clients at a sporting event and $600 for meals (not lavish) with a client where the taxpayer is present. For tax year 2025, what is the general deductibility?

options.text: Both the entertainment and the meals are fully deductible
Both the entertainment and the meals are nondeductible
The entertainment is nondeductible, and the business meal is generally 50% deductible
The entertainment is 50% deductible, and the meal is fully deductible

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Since the 2017 tax law, business entertainment expenses are generally nondeductible, while otherwise-qualifying business meals (not lavish, taxpayer present) are generally 50% deductible. Why the others are wrong: **A** entertainment is not deductible; **B** qualifying business meals remain 50% deductible, so 'both nondeductible' is wrong; **D** the deductibility is reversed—entertainment is disallowed and the meal is limited to 50%.

questions.stem: A single-member LLC owned by an individual makes no entity-classification election. By default, how is it treated for federal income tax purposes?

options.text: As a disregarded entity, with its activity reported on the owner's return
As a C corporation that must file Form 1120
As a partnership that must file Form 1065
As an S corporation by default

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the check-the-box rules, a domestic single-member LLC that makes no election is disregarded as separate from its owner, so an individual owner reports its activity on Schedule C (or the relevant schedule) of the owner's return. Why the others are wrong: **B** corporate treatment requires an affirmative election; **C** partnership treatment requires at least two members; **D** S status requires a separate election and eligibility, and is never the default.

questions.stem: A C corporation has a net operating loss (NOL) arising in a tax year beginning after 2020. Under current federal rules, how may the corporation generally use that NOL?

options.text: Carry it back five years and forward 20 years with no income limitation
Deduct it only in the year it arises or lose it entirely
Carry it back two years only, with no carryforward allowed
Carry it forward indefinitely, limited to 80% of taxable income in each carryforward year

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** For NOLs arising in tax years beginning after 2017 (post-CARES rules for years after 2020), the loss is carried forward indefinitely and the deduction in a carryforward year is limited to 80% of that year's taxable income (computed before the NOL). Why the others are wrong: **A** the general carryback was repealed and the indefinite carryforward replaced the 20-year rule; **B** unused NOLs carry forward, they are not lost; **C** there is no general two-year carryback for these NOLs.

questions.stem: An organization wants federal tax-exempt status as a charitable organization described in Internal Revenue Code Section 501(c)(3). Which characteristic is required?

options.text: It must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes, with no part of net earnings inuring to private shareholders or individuals
It must distribute its profits to its founders each year
It may devote a substantial part of its activities to influencing legislation without restriction
It must be a for-profit corporation that pays dividends

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A 501(c)(3) organization must be organized and operated exclusively for exempt purposes (e.g., charitable, religious, educational), and none of its net earnings may inure to the benefit of private shareholders or individuals. Why the others are wrong: **B** distributing profits to insiders violates the private-inurement prohibition; **C** lobbying may not be a substantial part of activities, and political campaign intervention is prohibited; **D** a 501(c)(3) is not a profit-distributing corporation.

questions.stem: Which two requirements must a corporation meet to be eligible to elect S corporation status? (Select two.)

options.text: It must have no more than 100 shareholders
It may have only one class of stock
It must have at least one nonresident alien shareholder
It must have at least two classes of common stock

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** To be an eligible S corporation, the entity must be a domestic corporation with no more than 100 shareholders and only one class of stock (differences solely in voting rights are allowed). Why the others are wrong: **C** shareholders must generally be U.S. citizens or residents—nonresident aliens are not permitted; **D** having more than one class of stock disqualifies the S election, so requiring two classes is wrong.

questions.stem: Which two items reduce a partner's outside basis in a partnership interest? (Select two.)

options.text: Cash distributions to the partner
The partner's distributive share of partnership taxable income
Additional cash the partner contributes to the partnership
The partner's distributive share of partnership losses

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, D):** A partner's outside basis is decreased by distributions received and by the partner's share of partnership losses and nondeductible expenses. Why the others are wrong: **B** a partner's share of partnership income increases outside basis; **C** additional contributions increase, not decrease, outside basis.

questions.stem: A decedent's estate earns $4,000 of taxable income during administration and distributes $4,000 to the sole beneficiary in the same year. Which statement best describes the federal income tax treatment of fiduciary income that is distributed?

options.text: The estate pays tax on all income and the beneficiary reports nothing
Neither the estate nor the beneficiary reports the income
The income is always tax-free because it passed through an estate
The estate receives a distribution deduction, and the beneficiary reports the income via a Schedule K-1

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Estates and trusts are conduits to the extent income is distributed; the fiduciary takes a distribution deduction (limited by distributable net income) and the beneficiary reports the distributed income on a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041). Why the others are wrong: **A** distributed income is taxed to the beneficiary, not retained at the estate level; **B** the income is taxable to someone—the estate on retained income or the beneficiary on distributed income; **C** income does not become tax-free merely by passing through an estate.

questions.stem: Which form does a partnership use to report its income, deductions, and other items to the IRS?

options.text: Form 1065, U.S. Return of Partnership Income
Form 1120, U.S. Corporation Income Tax Return
Form 1040, U.S. Individual Income Tax Return
Form 990, Return of Organization Exempt From Income Tax

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A partnership files Form 1065, an information return that reports the partnership's income and separately stated items and generates Schedules K-1 for the partners. Why the others are wrong: **B** Form 1120 is the C corporation income tax return; **C** Form 1040 is the individual income tax return; **D** Form 990 is filed by tax-exempt organizations.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants an enrolled agent to represent them before the IRS and to receive copies of confidential correspondence. Which form should be filed to authorize this representation?

options.text: Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative
Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization
Form 4506, Request for Copy of Tax Return
Form W-9, Request for Taxpayer Identification Number

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Form 2848 grants a power of attorney authorizing an eligible representative (such as an enrolled agent) to represent the taxpayer before the IRS and to receive confidential information for the matters listed. Why the others are wrong: **B** Form 8821 only authorizes disclosure of information—it does not permit representation or advocacy; **C** Form 4506 requests copies of returns; **D** Form W-9 provides a taxpayer identification number and has nothing to do with representation.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent holds a valid power of attorney. Which statement best describes the scope of an enrolled agent's authority to practice before the IRS?

options.text: Unlimited authority to represent any taxpayer before the IRS on any tax matter
Authority limited only to returns the agent personally prepared
Authority to represent taxpayers in U.S. Tax Court without further qualification
Authority limited to information requests but not examinations or appeals

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Enrolled agents have unlimited practice rights before the IRS—they may represent any taxpayer on any tax matter, including audits, collections, and appeals, regardless of who prepared the return. Why the others are wrong: **B** that limited scope describes annual filing season program participants, not enrolled agents; **C** representing taxpayers in Tax Court requires admission to that court, which is separate from IRS practice rights; **D** enrolled agents may handle examinations and appeals, not just information requests.

questions.stem: After an IRS examination results in a proposed adjustment the taxpayer disagrees with, the taxpayer wants an independent review without going to court first. To which body should the case generally be directed?

options.text: The U.S. Supreme Court
The Office of Professional Responsibility
The IRS Independent Office of Appeals
The Government Accountability Office

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The IRS Independent Office of Appeals provides an impartial administrative review of disputed examination results and seeks to resolve cases without litigation. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Supreme Court is the highest court and does not hear initial tax disputes; **B** the Office of Professional Responsibility oversees practitioner conduct, not taxpayer appeals; **D** the GAO audits federal agencies and does not resolve individual tax disputes.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who cannot pay a $30,000 assessed liability in full proposes to settle for less than the full amount because, based on income and assets, full collection is unlikely. Which collection alternative fits this situation?

options.text: A penalty abatement request
An amended return to reduce the tax
An information document request
An offer in compromise based on doubt as to collectibility

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An offer in compromise lets a taxpayer settle a liability for less than the full amount; doubt as to collectibility applies when the taxpayer's income and assets show the full amount is unlikely to be collected. Why the others are wrong: **A** penalty abatement removes penalties, not the underlying tax; **B** an amended return corrects errors—it does not negotiate a reduced payment on a correct liability; **C** an information document request is a tool examiners use to request records, not a collection settlement.

questions.stem: A taxpayer filed and paid late for the first time in many years of compliance and asks an enrolled agent how the failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties might be removed. Which relief is most directly applicable?

options.text: First-time abatement (FTA) administrative penalty relief
An offer in compromise based on doubt as to liability
A Collection Due Process hearing
Innocent spouse relief

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** First-time abatement is administrative relief from failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and failure-to-deposit penalties for a taxpayer with a clean compliance history (generally no penalties in the prior three years) who is otherwise current. Why the others are wrong: **B** doubt-as-to-liability offers dispute the tax owed, not penalties on an admitted late filing; **C** a CDP hearing addresses collection actions like liens and levies, not first-time penalty removal; **D** innocent spouse relief addresses joint-return liability allocation, not a sole filer's late-filing penalties.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is experiencing a significant hardship because of an unresolved IRS issue that normal channels have failed to fix. Which IRS-affiliated office is specifically designed to help in this situation?

options.text: The Taxpayer Advocate Service
The Criminal Investigation division
The Office of Chief Counsel
The Large Business and International division

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Taxpayer Advocate Service is an independent organization within the IRS that helps taxpayers experiencing financial hardship or who have not had problems resolved through normal channels. Why the others are wrong: **B** Criminal Investigation pursues tax crimes; **C** the Office of Chief Counsel provides legal guidance and litigates for the IRS; **D** LB&I administers tax for large and international taxpayers, not individual hardship assistance.

questions.stem: The IRS sends a taxpayer a statutory notice of deficiency. If the taxpayer wants to dispute the deficiency without first paying the tax, what is the general deadline and forum?

options.text: File a refund claim with the IRS within 30 days
Pay the tax immediately, then file in U.S. district court within 10 days
File a petition with the U.S. Tax Court within 90 days of the notice (150 days if addressed outside the U.S.)
There is no way to dispute a notice of deficiency

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A statutory notice of deficiency (90-day letter) lets the taxpayer petition the U.S. Tax Court within 90 days (150 if the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States) to dispute the deficiency without first paying it. Why the others are wrong: **A** disputing in Tax Court requires a petition, not a 30-day refund claim; **B** litigating in district court or the Court of Federal Claims requires first paying the tax and filing a refund suit, not a 10-day filing; **D** the notice specifically provides the right to petition the Tax Court.

questions.stem: Order the following stages of a typical individual income tax dispute from earliest to latest.

options.text: IRS examination (audit) of the return
Protest to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals
Issuance of a statutory notice of deficiency
Filing a petition in the U.S. Tax Court

questions.explanation: The usual progression is: the IRS first examines the return (A); if the taxpayer disagrees with the examiner's proposed adjustments, the case can be protested to the Independent Office of Appeals for an impartial administrative review (B); if no agreement is reached, the IRS issues a statutory notice of deficiency, the '90-day letter' (C); and the taxpayer may then petition the U.S. Tax Court to litigate without prepaying the tax (D). This order matters because Appeals is an administrative step before the deficiency notice, and the notice is the jurisdictional ticket that allows a Tax Court petition.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, a practitioner who learns that a client did not comply with the revenue laws or made an error or omission on a return must do what?

options.text: Immediately notify the IRS of the client's error without telling the client
Correct the client's prior return without the client's knowledge
Promptly advise the client of the noncompliance, error, or omission and the consequences
Ignore the issue because the practitioner did not prepare the return

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Circular 230 section 10.21 requires a practitioner who knows of a client's noncompliance, error, or omission to promptly advise the client of it and the consequences under the law and regulations. Why the others are wrong: **A** the practitioner is not required—or generally permitted—to report the client to the IRS; the duty runs to the client; **B** amending a return requires the client's consent; **D** the duty applies regardless of who prepared the return.

questions.stem: Which IRS office is responsible for matters of practitioner discipline and enforcing Circular 230 standards of conduct?

options.text: The Taxpayer Advocate Service
The Independent Office of Appeals
The Wage and Investment division
The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Office of Professional Responsibility administers and enforces Circular 230, with authority over the conduct and discipline (including censure, suspension, and disbarment) of practitioners before the IRS. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Taxpayer Advocate Service helps taxpayers resolve problems, not discipline practitioners; **B** Appeals reviews disputed tax matters; **C** the Wage and Investment division administers tax for individual filers, not practitioner discipline.

questions.stem: A paid preparer prepares a return claiming the earned income tax credit. To meet the due-diligence requirements and avoid the related preparer penalty, the preparer must do which of the following?

options.text: Complete and submit Form 8867, make reasonable inquiries for complete and consistent information, and keep records of the inquiries and documents relied on
Simply rely on whatever the client states, with no documentation
Guarantee the credit amount in writing to the client
Refuse to prepare any return claiming refundable credits

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Paid-preparer due diligence for the EITC (and CTC/ACTC, AOTC, and head-of-household status) requires completing Form 8867, applying the knowledge requirement by making reasonable inquiries when information seems incorrect or incomplete, computing the credit, and retaining records. Why the others are wrong: **B** blindly accepting client statements fails the knowledge requirement; **C** preparers do not guarantee credit amounts; **D** preparers may prepare such returns—they simply must perform due diligence.

questions.stem: A tax return preparer who prepares returns for compensation must obtain and use which identifier on returns they prepare?

options.text: The client's Social Security number in place of the preparer's
An Employer Identification Number for the taxpayer
A Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN)
No identifier is required for paid preparers

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Anyone who prepares or substantially helps prepare federal returns for compensation must have a current PTIN and include it on returns they prepare. Why the others are wrong: **A** a preparer must use their own PTIN, not the client's SSN; **B** an EIN identifies a business entity, not the paid preparer signing the return; **D** a PTIN is required, so 'no identifier' is wrong.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, which two actions can the Office of Professional Responsibility take against a practitioner who violates the regulations? (Select two.)

options.text: Sentence the practitioner to federal prison
Censure the practitioner
Suspend or disbar the practitioner from practice before the IRS
Revoke the practitioner's state driver's license

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, C):** Sanctions available under Circular 230 include censure (a public reprimand), suspension, disbarment, and monetary penalties imposed through OPR's disciplinary process. Why the others are wrong: **A** criminal imprisonment is imposed by the courts, not by OPR's administrative process; **D** OPR governs practice before the IRS and cannot revoke a state-issued driver's license.

questions.stem: Which two statements about electronic filing of federal individual returns are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: A preparer who reasonably expects to file 11 or more covered returns in a calendar year is generally required to e-file
A taxpayer may choose to opt out of e-file, and the preparer should document that choice
E-filing eliminates any need for the taxpayer to sign the return
Paid preparers are prohibited from ever filing paper returns

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The e-file mandate generally applies to specified tax return preparers who expect to file 11 or more covered returns in a year, and a taxpayer may elect to file on paper, with the preparer documenting that choice (e.g., Form 8948). Why the others are wrong: **C** the taxpayer must still sign, typically via Form 8879 for an e-filed return; **D** paper filing is still permitted in allowed circumstances, so an absolute prohibition is wrong.

questions.stem: A taxpayer's only income for the year is $1,200 of interest from a savings account. Which filing requirement concept determines whether the taxpayer must file a federal income tax return?

options.text: Whether the taxpayer received any Form 1099, regardless of amount
The taxpayer's net worth at year-end
Gross income compared to a threshold based on filing status and age
Whether the taxpayer expects a refund

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The general filing requirement turns on whether gross income meets or exceeds a threshold that varies by filing status, age, and (for dependents) the type of income; other rules can also force a return (e.g., self-employment earnings or advance premium tax credit reconciliation). Why the others are wrong: **A** receiving a 1099 does not by itself create a filing obligation if income is below the threshold; **B** net worth is irrelevant to the income-tax filing requirement; **D** expecting a refund may prompt a voluntary return but does not set the mandatory filing threshold.

questions.stem: An unmarried taxpayer's spouse died on March 1, 2025. They have no dependents and have not remarried. For tax year 2025, which filing status is generally most advantageous and available?

options.text: Married filing jointly for 2025
Qualifying surviving spouse for 2025
Head of household for 2025
Single for 2025

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A widow or widower is generally treated as married for the entire year of the spouse's death and may file a joint return for that year (here 2025) if not remarried by year-end. Why the others are wrong: **B** qualifying surviving spouse status applies in the two years after the year of death and requires a dependent child, neither of which is met for 2025; **C** head of household requires a qualifying person, and none exists here; **D** single is available but less favorable than the joint return allowed in the year of death.

questions.stem: A taxpayer received a state income tax refund in 2025 for state taxes paid in 2024. In 2024 the taxpayer claimed the standard deduction. How is the 2025 state refund treated federally?

options.text: Fully taxable in 2025 regardless of the prior year's deduction choice
Not taxable in 2025, because the taxpayer received no federal tax benefit from the state tax in 2024
Taxable, but only 50% of the refund is included
Taxable in 2024 by amending that year's return

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the tax benefit rule, a state income tax refund is includible in income only to the extent the prior-year state tax produced a federal tax benefit; because the taxpayer took the standard deduction in 2024, the state tax gave no benefit, so the refund is not taxable. Why the others are wrong: **A** taxability depends on whether the deduction was claimed and provided a benefit; **C** there is no automatic 50% inclusion rule; **D** any inclusion occurs in the year the refund is received, not by amending the prior year.

questions.stem: An employee receives nonqualified stock and other property. Which doctrine generally requires an item of income to be reported by the taxpayer who earned it, preventing assignment of that income to another person to reduce tax?

options.text: The constructive receipt doctrine
The assignment of income doctrine
The step transaction doctrine
The economic substance doctrine

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The assignment of income doctrine holds that income is taxed to the person who earns it (the tree that bears the fruit), so a taxpayer cannot avoid tax by directing earned income to be paid to someone else. Why the others are wrong: **A** constructive receipt addresses the timing of when cash-basis income is taxed, not who is taxed; **C** the step transaction doctrine collapses separate steps into one transaction; **D** the economic substance doctrine disallows transactions lacking a non-tax business purpose.

questions.stem: A taxpayer inherited shares of stock from a decedent who died in 2024. The decedent had a $5,000 basis, and the stock was worth $40,000 on the date of death. What is the beneficiary's basis in the inherited stock (no alternate valuation date elected)?

options.text: $5,000, a carryover of the decedent's basis
$40,000, the fair market value on the date of death (stepped-up basis)
$0, because inherited property has no basis
$22,500, the average of the decedent's basis and fair market value

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Property acquired from a decedent generally takes a basis equal to its fair market value on the date of death (or the alternate valuation date if elected), so the beneficiary's basis is $40,000—a step-up that erases the pre-death appreciation. Why the others are wrong: **A** carryover basis applies to gifts, not inheritances; **C** inherited property does have a basis; **D** there is no averaging convention—basis is the date-of-death value.

questions.stem: A donor gives a friend stock with a fair market value of $8,000 at the time of the gift. The donor's adjusted basis was $10,000. The friend later sells the stock for $7,000. What gain or loss does the friend recognize?

options.text: A $3,000 loss, using the donor's $10,000 basis
A $1,000 loss, using the $8,000 fair market value at the date of the gift
A $1,000 gain, using the donor's $10,000 basis
No gain or loss, because the sale price falls between the two basis figures

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the dual-basis rule for gifts of depreciated property, the donee uses the donor's basis to figure gain and the lower fair market value at the date of gift to figure loss; selling at $7,000 (below the $8,000 FMV) produces a $1,000 loss. Why the others are wrong: **A** loss is measured against the $8,000 FMV, not the $10,000 donor basis; **C** a sale below the FMV results in a loss, not a gain; **D** the no-gain-no-loss zone applies only when the sale price falls between the FMV and the donor's basis—$7,000 is below both.

questions.stem: For tax year 2025, a taxpayer wants to deduct unreimbursed medical expenses as an itemized deduction. Which rule governs the deductible amount?

options.text: Only the portion of qualified medical expenses exceeding 7.5% of adjusted gross income is deductible
All qualified medical expenses are deductible with no floor
Medical expenses are deductible only as an above-the-line adjustment
Medical expenses are limited to a flat $2,500 per return

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Unreimbursed qualified medical and dental expenses are deductible as an itemized deduction only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of adjusted gross income. Why the others are wrong: **B** a percentage-of-AGI floor applies, so not all expenses are deductible; **C** medical expenses are an itemized deduction, not an above-the-line adjustment; **D** there is no flat dollar cap on the medical deduction—the limit is the AGI-based floor.

questions.stem: A taxpayer pays $2,000 of interest on a qualified student loan during 2025 and is not a dependent of anyone else. Ignoring income phase-outs, how is this generally treated?

options.text: As a nonrefundable credit equal to the full interest paid
As a miscellaneous itemized deduction subject to a 2% floor
As entirely nondeductible personal interest
As an above-the-line adjustment to income, up to $2,500 per year

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Qualified student loan interest is deductible as an above-the-line adjustment of up to $2,500 per year (subject to income phase-outs), so the full $2,000 is deductible here. Why the others are wrong: **A** it is a deduction, not a credit; **B** it is an adjustment to income, not a miscellaneous itemized deduction; **C** although most personal interest is nondeductible, student loan interest is a specific statutory exception.

questions.stem: A taxpayer has wages plus a large amount of long-term capital gains and qualified dividends, and is subject to the alternative minimum tax (AMT). What is the basic purpose of the AMT?

options.text: To impose a second tax on income already taxed at regular rates with no offset
To ensure taxpayers with substantial economic income pay at least a minimum amount of tax by limiting certain preferences and deductions
To replace the regular tax for all taxpayers each year
To tax only tax-exempt municipal bond interest

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The AMT is a parallel system that recomputes taxable income by adding back or limiting certain preference items and deductions, applying an exemption and AMT rates, so taxpayers with significant economic income cannot avoid paying a minimum tax. Why the others are wrong: **A** the taxpayer pays the greater of regular tax or tentative minimum tax—it is not simply double taxation; **C** AMT applies only when it exceeds the regular tax, not as a universal replacement; **D** AMT addresses many items, and only certain private-activity bond interest is a preference, not all municipal interest.

questions.stem: Two parents are divorced. Their child lived with the mother (the custodial parent) for most of the year. The noncustodial father wants to claim the child as a dependent. What is generally required for the father to do so?

options.text: Nothing extra; the higher-earning parent automatically claims the child
The custodial parent must release the dependency claim in writing, generally on Form 8332, which the noncustodial parent attaches to the return
The father must have provided 100% of the child's support
Both parents must claim the child and let the IRS allocate it

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents, the custodial parent generally has the dependency claim but may release it to the noncustodial parent in a written declaration, typically Form 8332, attached to the noncustodial parent's return. Why the others are wrong: **A** earnings alone do not determine the claim; the tie-breaker and release rules govern; **C** providing all support is not the test—the release is; **D** the child cannot be claimed by both parents; a release prevents the conflict.

questions.stem: A taxpayer contributes to a Roth IRA. Assuming the account has been open more than five years and the taxpayer is over age 59½, how are qualified distributions of earnings treated?

options.text: Fully taxable as ordinary income when withdrawn
Tax-free, because qualified Roth distributions of earnings are excluded from gross income
Taxable only to the extent of the original contributions
Subject to a mandatory 20% withholding as taxable income

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A qualified distribution from a Roth IRA—one made after the five-year period and after the owner reaches 59½ (or meets another qualifying event)—is entirely tax-free, including the earnings. Why the others are wrong: **A** qualified Roth earnings are not taxable; **C** contributions were already after-tax and come out tax-free, and qualified earnings are also tax-free; **D** qualified Roth distributions are not taxable income, so no income-tax withholding applies.

questions.stem: Which two types of income are generally included in a taxpayer's gross income for federal income tax purposes? (Select two.)

options.text: Jury duty pay received by the taxpayer
Child support payments received
Cancellation of nonbusiness debt for which no exclusion applies
A gift of cash from a family member

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** Jury duty pay is taxable compensation, and cancellation of indebtedness income is generally included in gross income unless a specific exclusion (such as insolvency or qualified principal residence relief) applies. Why the others are wrong: **B** child support is neither taxable to the recipient nor deductible by the payer; **D** a bona fide gift is excluded from the recipient's gross income.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen donor makes gifts during 2025. Which two statements about the federal gift tax are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: Gifts that qualify for the annual exclusion (a per-donee amount, $19,000 for 2025) are not taxable gifts
Tuition paid directly to an educational institution for someone is an excludable transfer
The donee is primarily liable for paying any federal gift tax
All gifts of any size must have gift tax paid immediately at the time of the gift

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Gifts within the annual exclusion (for 2025, $19,000 per donee) are not taxable gifts, and amounts paid directly to a school for tuition (or to a provider for medical care) are excluded entirely under the qualified-transfer rule. Why the others are wrong: **C** the donor, not the donee, is primarily liable for the gift tax; **D** because of the annual exclusion and the lifetime unified credit, most gifts generate no gift tax due at the time of transfer.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen lives and works abroad all year and meets the bona fide residence or physical presence test. Which provision may allow them to exclude a limited amount of foreign-earned wages from U.S. gross income?

options.text: The foreign earned income exclusion
The standard deduction for nonresidents
The dividends-received deduction
The qualified business income deduction

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A qualifying U.S. citizen or resident living abroad who meets the bona fide residence or physical presence test may elect the foreign earned income exclusion to exclude a limited amount of foreign earned income (the limit is indexed annually). Why the others are wrong: **B** there is no special 'nonresident standard deduction' that excludes foreign wages, and the taxpayer here is a U.S. citizen taxed on worldwide income; **C** the dividends-received deduction is a corporate provision; **D** the QBI deduction relates to qualified business income, not the exclusion of foreign wages.

questions.stem: A C corporation owns 10% of the stock of an unrelated domestic taxable corporation and receives a $100,000 dividend from it. Which federal tax provision generally reduces the recipient corporation's tax on that dividend?

options.text: The qualified business income deduction
The foreign tax credit
The dividends-received deduction (DRD)
The charitable contribution deduction

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A C corporation that receives dividends from another domestic taxable corporation may claim a dividends-received deduction (a percentage that depends on the ownership stake) to mitigate triple taxation of corporate earnings. Why the others are wrong: **A** the QBI deduction is for noncorporate owners of pass-through income, not C corporations; **B** the foreign tax credit relates to foreign taxes paid, not domestic dividends; **D** the charitable contribution deduction applies to gifts to charity, not to received dividends.

questions.stem: A new business incurs $3,000 of qualifying start-up costs before opening its doors. For federal tax purposes, how are start-up expenditures generally treated?

options.text: They are never deductible because they precede operations
A limited amount may be deducted in the first year, with the remainder amortized over 180 months
They must be added to the basis of the owner's stock and never recovered
They are fully deductible only if the business later fails

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A business may elect to deduct a limited amount of qualifying start-up (and organizational) costs in the year it begins operations and amortize any remainder ratably over 180 months. Why the others are wrong: **A** start-up costs are recoverable through the first-year deduction and amortization; **C** they are not permanently capitalized into stock basis without recovery; **D** the deduction and amortization apply to operating businesses, not only to failed ones.

questions.stem: A taxpayer transfers appreciated property to a newly formed corporation solely in exchange for stock and, immediately after the exchange, owns 90% of the corporation's stock. Under Section 351, what is the general tax result?

options.text: Gain is fully recognized because any transfer to a corporation is taxable
No gain or loss is recognized because the transferor is in control (at least 80%) immediately after the exchange
Only half the realized gain is recognized
Loss is recognized but gain is deferred

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Section 351 provides nonrecognition when one or more persons transfer property to a corporation solely for stock and, immediately after, the transferors control the corporation (own at least 80% of voting power and stock); the 90% ownership here meets the control test. Why the others are wrong: **A** not every transfer to a corporation is taxable—the control requirement triggers deferral; **C** there is no general half-gain recognition rule; **D** when no boot is received, neither gain nor loss is recognized—loss is not separately recognized.

questions.stem: A business buys office furniture (7-year property) and places it in service in the current year. The owner wants to immediately expense the cost rather than depreciate it over several years. Which provision generally allows an election to do so, subject to dollar and taxable-income limits?

options.text: Section 1031 like-kind exchange treatment
Section 121 exclusion
Section 179 expensing
Section 1244 stock treatment

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Section 179 lets a business elect to expense the cost of qualifying tangible personal property placed in service during the year, subject to an annual dollar limit, an investment phase-out, and a taxable-income limitation. Why the others are wrong: **A** Section 1031 defers gain on like-kind exchanges of real property, not current expensing of furniture; **B** Section 121 excludes gain on a personal residence; **D** Section 1244 allows ordinary loss treatment on certain small business stock, unrelated to expensing equipment.

questions.stem: A business owns real estate used in its trade and exchanges it for other real property to be held for business use, qualifying under Section 1031. It receives $20,000 of cash (boot) in addition to the replacement real property, and its realized gain is $50,000. How much gain is recognized?

options.text: $50,000, the entire realized gain
$0, because like-kind exchanges are always fully tax-free
$20,000, the gain recognized to the extent of the boot received
$30,000, the realized gain minus the boot

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** In a like-kind exchange of real property, realized gain is recognized only to the extent of boot received—here the $20,000 cash—while the remaining gain is deferred. Why the others are wrong: **A** the full gain is not recognized when the exchange otherwise qualifies under Section 1031; **B** receipt of boot triggers recognition, so it is not fully tax-free; **D** recognized gain equals the lesser of boot or realized gain ($20,000), not realized gain reduced by boot.

questions.stem: An accrual-method retailer sells goods. Under the all-events test, when is income generally recognized for federal tax purposes?

options.text: When all events have occurred that fix the right to receive the income and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy
Only when cash is actually collected from the customer
When the business decides it wishes to report the income
When the goods are first ordered, regardless of delivery

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Under the accrual method's all-events test, income is recognized when all events fixing the right to receive it have occurred and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy, generally tied to the earlier of when earned, due, or received. Why the others are wrong: **B** awaiting actual collection is the cash method, not accrual; **C** recognition is governed by the test, not by election of timing; **D** merely ordering goods does not fix the right to income before performance or delivery.

questions.stem: An employer pays wages to employees and must report those wages and withheld taxes to the federal government each quarter. Which federal form is generally used for this quarterly reporting?

options.text: Form 941, Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return
Form 1099-NEC, Nonemployee Compensation
Form 1120-S, U.S. Income Tax Return for an S Corporation
Form 706, United States Estate Tax Return

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Employers generally report wages paid and federal income tax, Social Security, and Medicare taxes withheld each quarter on Form 941. Why the others are wrong: **B** Form 1099-NEC reports payments to nonemployee independent contractors, not employee wages; **C** Form 1120-S is the S corporation income tax return; **D** Form 706 is the estate tax return, unrelated to quarterly payroll reporting.

questions.stem: A business hires a worker and must decide whether the worker is an employee or an independent contractor. Which framework does the IRS primarily use to make this determination?

options.text: Whether the worker requests employee status in writing
Solely whether the worker is paid hourly or by the project
Whether the business issued the worker a Form W-2 last year
Common-law factors examining behavioral control, financial control, and the relationship of the parties

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** Worker classification turns on common-law control factors grouped into behavioral control, financial control, and the type of relationship; no single factor is decisive. Why the others are wrong: **A** the worker's preference does not control the legal classification; **B** the method of payment is just one financial-control factor, not the whole test; **C** prior issuance of a W-2 does not by itself establish current status—the substantive control factors govern.

questions.stem: A farmer uses the cash method and wants to even out fluctuating income across years. Which special federal tax provision is uniquely available to farmers and certain fishermen?

options.text: Income averaging using Schedule J for elected farm income
A permanent exemption from all federal income tax on farm income
Mandatory use of the accrual method for all farm operations
A flat 10% tax rate on all farm profits

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Farmers (and certain commercial fishermen) may elect farm income averaging on Schedule J, spreading elected farm income back over the three prior years' brackets to smooth tax in high-income years. Why the others are wrong: **B** farm income is taxable; there is no blanket exemption; **C** many farmers may use the cash method—accrual is not universally required; **D** there is no special flat rate on farm profits.

questions.stem: A tax-exempt 501(c)(3) organization operates a regularly carried-on trade or business that is not substantially related to its exempt purpose. What is the federal tax consequence of the net income from that activity?

options.text: It is always tax-free because the organization is exempt
It is generally subject to the unrelated business income tax (UBIT)
It automatically revokes the organization's exempt status
It is taxed only if distributed to the organization's officers

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Net income from a regularly carried-on trade or business that is not substantially related to an exempt organization's purpose is generally taxed as unrelated business taxable income (UBIT), reported on Form 990-T. Why the others are wrong: **A** exemption does not shield unrelated business income; **C** earning some unrelated income does not automatically revoke exemption unless it becomes the organization's primary activity; **D** UBIT applies to the income itself, not only upon distribution to insiders.

questions.stem: Which two items increase a shareholder's stock basis in an S corporation? (Select two.)

options.text: Distributions of cash the shareholder receives from the corporation
The shareholder's pro rata share of the S corporation's separately stated and nonseparately stated income
Additional capital the shareholder contributes to the corporation
The shareholder's pro rata share of the corporation's deductible losses

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, C):** An S corporation shareholder's stock basis increases by the shareholder's share of the corporation's income items and by additional capital contributions. Why the others are wrong: **A** distributions reduce stock basis; **D** the shareholder's share of losses and deductions reduces basis (and is limited by basis), so it does not increase it.

questions.stem: A complex trust earns dividends and interest during the year and is permitted to accumulate income. What does distributable net income (DNI) primarily limit for federal tax purposes?

options.text: The total amount the trustee may invest in any one security
The maximum distribution deduction for the trust and the amount taxable to the beneficiaries
The number of beneficiaries the trust may have
The trust's exposure to the estate tax

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Distributable net income caps both the trust's (or estate's) distribution deduction and the amount of distributed income taxable to beneficiaries, and it also determines the character of the income they report. Why the others are wrong: **A** DNI is a tax concept, not an investment-concentration limit; **C** DNI does not restrict the number of beneficiaries; **D** DNI relates to fiduciary income tax, not the estate tax.

questions.stem: An employer sponsors a 401(k) plan, which is a qualified retirement plan. Which statement best describes a key federal tax feature of employee elective deferrals to a traditional 401(k)?

options.text: Deferrals are made with after-tax dollars and grow tax-free with no limits
Pre-tax elective deferrals reduce current taxable wages, and the deferred amounts and earnings are taxed when distributed
Deferrals are fully taxable now and again at distribution
Employees may defer an unlimited amount each year

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Traditional pre-tax 401(k) elective deferrals reduce the employee's current taxable wages, grow tax-deferred, and are taxed as ordinary income when distributed. Why the others are wrong: **A** that describes designated Roth contributions, and deferrals are subject to annual limits; **C** pre-tax deferrals are not taxed currently, so there is no double taxation; **D** elective deferrals are capped by an annual statutory limit.

questions.stem: The IRS files a federal tax lien against a taxpayer and is preparing to levy. The taxpayer wants an independent hearing to propose collection alternatives and challenge the action. Which procedure provides this right?

options.text: A request for a private letter ruling
A petition to the U.S. Supreme Court
A Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing
A Freedom of Information Act request

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A Collection Due Process hearing, available after a Notice of Federal Tax Lien filing or a final notice of intent to levy, lets the taxpayer raise collection alternatives and certain liability issues before the Independent Office of Appeals, with limited judicial review. Why the others are wrong: **A** a private letter ruling addresses prospective tax treatment, not collection disputes; **B** the Supreme Court does not hold initial collection hearings; **D** a FOIA request obtains records and is not a collection hearing.

questions.stem: A taxpayer cannot pay a tax liability in full now but can pay it over time through monthly payments. Which arrangement allows the taxpayer to satisfy the liability on a schedule?

options.text: A statutory notice of deficiency
An information document request
A closing agreement on a different tax year
An installment agreement

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An installment agreement lets a taxpayer who cannot pay in full satisfy the liability through monthly payments over time; certain balances qualify for streamlined approval. Why the others are wrong: **A** a notice of deficiency proposes additional tax—it is not a payment plan; **B** an information document request seeks records during an examination; **C** a closing agreement finalizes specific tax matters, not a routine payment schedule for an existing balance.

questions.stem: A spouse signed a joint return without knowing the other spouse understated income, and it would be unfair to hold the requesting spouse liable for the resulting deficiency. Which form is generally used to request relief?

options.text: Form 8857, Request for Innocent Spouse Relief
Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative
Form 656, Offer in Compromise
Form 9465, Installment Agreement Request

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** A spouse seeking relief from joint and several liability on a joint return because of the other spouse's erroneous items files Form 8857 to request innocent spouse relief. Why the others are wrong: **B** Form 2848 authorizes representation, not liability relief; **C** Form 656 proposes settling a liability for less than the full amount, a different remedy; **D** Form 9465 requests an installment plan, not relief from the underlying joint liability.

questions.stem: During an examination, the IRS proposes adjustments and issues a letter giving the taxpayer 30 days to request a conference with Appeals before a notice of deficiency is issued. This letter is commonly known as what?

options.text: A 90-day letter
A summons
A 30-day letter
A demand for payment

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The 30-day letter accompanies the examiner's report and gives the taxpayer 30 days to request an Appeals conference before the IRS issues a statutory notice of deficiency. Why the others are wrong: **A** the 90-day letter is the statutory notice of deficiency that follows if no agreement is reached; **B** a summons compels testimony or records, not an Appeals conference; **D** a demand for payment is a collection notice issued after assessment, not a pre-assessment appeal opportunity.

questions.stem: Which document is the IRS's plain-language summary of the fundamental rights every taxpayer has when dealing with the agency, such as the right to be informed and the right to appeal?

options.text: The Internal Revenue Manual's penalty handbook
Circular 230
The Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
The Taxpayer Bill of Rights

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Taxpayer Bill of Rights groups existing taxpayer protections into ten fundamental rights, including the right to be informed, to quality service, to challenge the IRS's position, and to appeal. Why the others are wrong: **A** the penalty handbook guides IRS employees on penalties, not a statement of taxpayer rights; **B** Circular 230 governs practitioners' conduct, not taxpayer rights; **C** GAAP is a body of financial accounting standards unrelated to taxpayer rights.

questions.stem: Which two practitioners generally have unlimited rights to represent taxpayers before the IRS? (Select two.)

options.text: An enrolled agent in active status
A certified public accountant (CPA) authorized to practice
An unenrolled preparer who only participates in the Annual Filing Season Program
A friend with a financial power of attorney but no credential

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Enrolled agents, CPAs, and attorneys are the credentialed practitioners with unlimited representation rights before the IRS. Why the others are wrong: **C** Annual Filing Season Program participants have only limited representation rights, generally before revenue agents and customer service for returns they prepared and signed; **D** a general power of attorney without an eligible credential does not confer unlimited representation rights before the IRS.

questions.stem: Order the following steps in establishing authority and beginning representation of a taxpayer in an IRS examination, from earliest to latest.

options.text: Confirm the practitioner is eligible to practice (e.g., active enrolled agent with a valid PTIN)
Obtain a signed Form 2848 power of attorney from the taxpayer for the years and matters at issue
Submit or present the authorization to the IRS so the practitioner can receive information and communicate on the taxpayer's behalf
Respond to the examiner's information requests and advocate for the taxpayer

questions.explanation: The logical sequence is: first confirm the practitioner is actually eligible to practice before the IRS, such as being an enrolled agent in active status with a valid PTIN (A); then obtain a signed Form 2848 covering the specific taxpayer, tax years, and matters (B); next get that authorization on file with or presented to the IRS so the practitioner may receive confidential information and speak for the taxpayer (C); and only then respond to the examiner's requests and advocate the taxpayer's position (D). The order matters because a practitioner cannot lawfully receive the taxpayer's information or act until eligibility is established and a valid authorization is in place.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, when may a practitioner generally charge a contingent fee in connection with a matter before the IRS?

options.text: For preparing an original tax return, as a percentage of the refund claimed
In limited circumstances, such as for services in connection with an IRS examination or challenge to an original return, or a claim for refund filed in connection with a statutory interest or penalty
For any service whatsoever, with no restrictions
Never, because all fees must be hourly

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Circular 230 section 10.27 generally prohibits contingent fees but allows them in limited situations, such as services rendered in connection with an IRS examination of, or challenge to, an original return, or certain refund claims tied to statutory interest or penalties. Why the others are wrong: **A** charging a contingent fee for preparing an original return as a percentage of the refund is precisely what the rule forbids; **C** contingent fees are restricted, not unlimited; **D** fees need not be hourly—fixed and other reasonable fee arrangements are permitted.

questions.stem: A former client asks a practitioner to return the client's original records so the client can comply with a filing deadline, but the practitioner is owed unpaid fees. Under Circular 230, what must the practitioner generally do?

options.text: Keep all records until the fee dispute is fully resolved, regardless of state law
Promptly return the client's records necessary to comply with federal tax obligations, even if a fee dispute exists
Destroy the records to protect confidentiality
Forward the records directly to the IRS instead of the client

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Circular 230 section 10.28 generally requires a practitioner to promptly return a client's records necessary for the client to comply with federal tax obligations upon request, even when a fee dispute exists (though a permitted state-law retaining lien may apply to certain practitioner-prepared work product). Why the others are wrong: **A** the duty to return the client's own records is not suspended merely because fees are unpaid; **C** destroying client records is improper; **D** the records belong to the client and should be returned to the client, not sent to the IRS.
