questions.stem: A practitioner takes a position on a client's return that is contrary to a clear IRS rule. To avoid the Section 6694 preparer penalty for an unreasonable position that is not disclosed, the position generally must meet which standard?

options.text: Any position the client requests, regardless of merit
Substantial authority for an undisclosed non-tax-shelter position (or a reasonable basis if adequately disclosed)
Only a frivolous-but-arguable position
A position with less than a 5% chance of success

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** To avoid the Section 6694 penalty, an undisclosed position (other than a tax shelter or reportable transaction) generally needs substantial authority, while a disclosed position generally needs at least a reasonable basis. Why the others are wrong: **A** merely following the client's wishes does not satisfy the standard; **C** a frivolous position fails the standard and can itself trigger penalties; **D** a very low probability of success does not meet substantial authority or reasonable basis.

questions.stem: A taxpayer needs more time to file a Form 1040 and timely files for an automatic extension. Which statement best describes the effect of the extension?

options.text: It extends both the time to file and the time to pay, with no interest
It eliminates the need to file the return at all that year
It extends the time to file the return but not the time to pay any tax owed
It is available only to taxpayers who are due a refund

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** An automatic filing extension (via Form 4868) extends the deadline to file the return but not the deadline to pay; tax not paid by the original due date accrues interest and may incur a failure-to-pay penalty. Why the others are wrong: **A** the extension does not extend the time to pay, and interest still runs on unpaid amounts; **B** the return must still be filed by the extended due date; **D** an extension is available regardless of whether the taxpayer expects a refund or owes tax.

questions.stem: A business pays an independent contractor $2,000 for services during the year in the course of its trade or business. Which information return must the business generally file to report these nonemployee payments?

options.text: Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement
Form 1098, Mortgage Interest Statement
Form 1099-NEC, Nonemployee Compensation
Form 1095-A, Health Insurance Marketplace Statement

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** Payments of $600 or more for services to a nonemployee in the course of a trade or business are generally reported on Form 1099-NEC. Why the others are wrong: **A** Form W-2 reports wages paid to employees, not payments to independent contractors; **B** Form 1098 reports mortgage interest received; **D** Form 1095-A reports Marketplace health coverage, unrelated to contractor payments.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, which two duties or restrictions apply to a practitioner's conduct? (Select two.)

options.text: The practitioner may freely use false or misleading advertising to attract clients
The practitioner must exercise due diligence in preparing and filing returns and in determining the correctness of representations made to the IRS
The practitioner may negotiate a taxpayer's IRS refund check issued to the client
The practitioner must not unreasonably delay the prompt disposition of any matter before the IRS

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** Circular 230 requires practitioners to exercise due diligence (section 10.22) and prohibits unreasonably delaying the prompt disposition of matters before the IRS (section 10.23). Why the others are wrong: **A** false or misleading advertising and solicitation are prohibited under section 10.30; **C** a practitioner must not endorse or otherwise negotiate a taxpayer's refund check under section 10.31.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who is required to file a 2025 individual income tax return needs a tax identification number but is a nonresident alien who is ineligible for a Social Security number. What number should the taxpayer obtain to file?

options.text: A Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN)
An Employer Identification Number (EIN)
An Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN)
No number is needed; the taxpayer may file without any identifier

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A person who must file a U.S. return but cannot get a Social Security number applies for an ITIN on Form W-7, which the IRS issues solely for federal tax purposes. Why the others are wrong: **A** a PTIN is for paid preparers, not for a taxpayer filing their own return; **B** an EIN identifies a business entity, not an individual filer; **D** a return requires a valid identifying number, so filing with none is not allowed.

questions.stem: An unmarried taxpayer's elderly mother lives in her own apartment, and the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of maintaining that household for her mother, who qualifies as the taxpayer's dependent. Can the taxpayer claim head of household status?

options.text: No, because the qualifying person must always physically live in the taxpayer's own home
Yes, because a dependent parent need not live with the taxpayer if the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of keeping up the parent's main home
No, because head of household is available only to taxpayers with a qualifying child
Yes, but only if the mother also lived with the taxpayer for the entire year

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A dependent parent is a special case: the taxpayer can qualify for head of household by paying more than half the cost of keeping up the parent's main home (such as the parent's own apartment) even though the parent does not live with the taxpayer. Why the others are wrong: **A** the live-in requirement is waived specifically for a dependent parent; **C** a qualifying relative such as a parent can support head of household, not only a qualifying child; **D** the parent is not required to live with the taxpayer at all.

questions.stem: An employer provides an employee group-term life insurance coverage. Which statement correctly describes the federal income tax treatment of this fringe benefit?

options.text: The cost of all employer-provided group-term life insurance is fully taxable to the employee
The cost of coverage up to $50,000 is excludable, and the cost of coverage exceeding $50,000 is included in the employee's income
Group-term life insurance is always entirely tax-free regardless of the coverage amount
Only the death benefit is taxable, never the cost of coverage

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An employee may exclude the cost of the first $50,000 of employer-provided group-term life insurance; the cost of coverage above $50,000 (figured under an IRS table) is included in wages. Why the others are wrong: **A** coverage up to $50,000 is excludable, so it is not all taxable; **C** coverage above $50,000 produces taxable income, so it is not entirely tax-free; **D** the includible item is the cost of excess coverage, and life insurance death proceeds are generally tax-free, so the statement is backwards.

questions.stem: A taxpayer who actively participates in a residential rental real estate activity has a $30,000 loss for the year and modified adjusted gross income of $90,000 from wages. The taxpayer is not a real estate professional. How much of the rental loss may generally be deducted against nonpassive income for 2025?

options.text: The full $30,000, because rental losses are always fully deductible
$0, because all rental losses are passive and may never offset wages
Up to $25,000 under the active participation exception to the passive loss rules
Exactly $3,000, the same as the capital loss limit

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A taxpayer who actively participates in rental real estate may deduct up to $25,000 of loss against nonpassive income; that allowance phases out between $100,000 and $150,000 of MAGI, so at $90,000 MAGI the full $25,000 is available. Why the others are wrong: **A** rental real estate is generally passive, so losses are limited; **B** the active participation exception specifically allows up to $25,000, so it is not always zero; **D** the $3,000 figure is the capital loss limit, which is unrelated to passive rental losses.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wins $4,000 gambling at a casino during 2025 and has $5,000 of documented gambling losses for the year. The taxpayer itemizes deductions. How are the winnings and losses reported?

options.text: Net the two and report a $1,000 loss as an adjustment to income
Report $4,000 of winnings in income and deduct gambling losses as an itemized deduction, but only up to the $4,000 of winnings
Report nothing, because gambling winnings and losses always cancel out
Report $4,000 of winnings and deduct the full $5,000 of losses

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Gambling winnings are fully includible in gross income, and gambling losses are deductible only as an itemized deduction and only to the extent of gambling winnings—here capped at $4,000. Why the others are wrong: **A** winnings and losses cannot be netted, and losses are not an above-the-line adjustment; **C** winnings must be reported in full and do not simply cancel against losses; **D** the loss deduction cannot exceed the $4,000 of winnings, so the excess $1,000 is not deductible.

questions.stem: A taxpayer makes a $6,000 cash contribution to a qualified public charity and also donates publicly traded stock held for three years with a fair market value of $10,000 and a basis of $4,000. For long-term appreciated stock donated to a public charity, what is the general amount of the charitable deduction?

options.text: The donor's $4,000 cost basis in the stock
The $10,000 fair market value of the stock at the date of the gift
The $6,000 of appreciation only
Zero, because gifts of property are not deductible

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A gift of long-term capital gain property, such as appreciated publicly traded stock, to a public charity is generally deductible at its fair market value—$10,000—without recognizing the built-in gain (subject to a 30%-of-AGI limit). Why the others are wrong: **A** basis is used for short-term property or ordinary-income property, not long-term appreciated stock; **C** the deduction is the full fair market value, not just the appreciation; **D** property contributions to qualified charities are deductible.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is enrolled in a high-deductible health plan and contributes to a Health Savings Account (HSA). Which statement best describes a key federal tax benefit of HSA contributions?

options.text: Contributions are nondeductible and all distributions are taxable
Contributions are deductible only if the taxpayer itemizes
HSAs may be funded by anyone regardless of health plan coverage
Deductible contributions reduce gross income, and qualified medical distributions are tax-free

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** An eligible individual's HSA contributions are deductible above the line (or excludable if made through an employer), the account grows tax-deferred, and distributions used for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. Why the others are wrong: **A** contributions are deductible and qualified distributions are tax-free; **B** the HSA deduction is an above-the-line adjustment, not an itemized deduction; **C** only individuals covered by a qualifying high-deductible health plan (and meeting other rules) may contribute.

questions.stem: A taxpayer is the original holder of a traditional IRA and reaches the age at which lifetime required minimum distributions must begin. If the taxpayer fails to take the full required minimum distribution for the year, what is the federal tax consequence on the shortfall under current law?

options.text: There is no consequence; RMDs are optional
An excise tax applies to the amount not distributed (generally 25%, reducible to 10% if timely corrected)
The entire IRA becomes immediately taxable in full
A flat $500 penalty applies regardless of the shortfall

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** If a taxpayer does not take the full required minimum distribution, an excise tax applies to the shortfall—generally 25% under current law, reduced to 10% if the failure is corrected within the applicable correction window. Why the others are wrong: **A** lifetime RMDs from a traditional IRA are mandatory once they begin; **C** only the missed distribution (not the whole account) is at issue, plus the excise tax; **D** the penalty is a percentage of the undistributed amount, not a flat $500.

questions.stem: A working couple files jointly and pays $7,000 in 2025 for after-school care for their 8-year-old child so both spouses can work. They want to claim the child and dependent care credit. Which condition must be met?

options.text: The credit is available even if neither spouse has any earned income
The care must be for a child who is at least 13 years old
Both spouses must have earned income (unless a spouse is a student or disabled), and the care must enable them to work or look for work
The credit may be claimed only by taxpayers who do not work

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The child and dependent care credit requires that the expenses enable the taxpayer (and spouse, if married filing jointly) to work or look for work, and both spouses generally must have earned income unless one is a full-time student or incapable of self-care. Why the others are wrong: **A** earned income (with the student/disabled exceptions) is required; **B** the qualifying child must be under age 13, not 13 or older; **D** the credit exists precisely because the care lets the taxpayer work, so 'only for those who do not work' is wrong.

questions.stem: A high-income single taxpayer has $250,000 of wages and $40,000 of net investment income (interest, dividends, and capital gains). Which additional federal tax may apply specifically to the investment income?

options.text: The 3.8% net investment income tax on the lesser of net investment income or the excess of modified AGI over the threshold
A 10% early withdrawal penalty on the dividends
Self-employment tax on the investment income
No additional tax can ever apply to investment income

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The net investment income tax imposes an extra 3.8% on the lesser of net investment income or the amount by which modified AGI exceeds the threshold for the filing status, which a high-income taxpayer with substantial investment income can owe. Why the others are wrong: **B** the 10% additional tax applies to early retirement distributions, not ordinary investment income; **C** investment income is not subject to self-employment tax; **D** the net investment income tax can clearly apply, so 'never' is wrong.

questions.stem: A taxpayer realizes a $9,000 net capital loss for the year and has no capital gains. How does this loss affect the current-year individual return, and what happens to any excess?

options.text: The full $9,000 is deductible against ordinary income this year
Up to $3,000 of the net capital loss offsets ordinary income this year, and the remaining $6,000 carries forward to future years
None of the loss is deductible and none carries forward
The loss must be carried back three years before any can be used

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An individual may deduct net capital losses against ordinary income only up to $3,000 per year ($1,500 if married filing separately); the unused $6,000 carries forward indefinitely to offset future gains and, subject to the limit, ordinary income. Why the others are wrong: **A** the annual offset against ordinary income is capped at $3,000; **C** the loss is partly deductible now and the rest carries forward, so it is not lost; **D** individual net capital losses carry forward, not back.

questions.stem: A client tells an enrolled agent he wants to deduct the value of the time he donated volunteering at a charity and the cost of commuting to his regular job. Advising the individual taxpayer, which statement is correct?

options.text: Both the value of donated services and commuting costs are deductible
Neither the value of donated personal services nor ordinary commuting costs to a regular workplace are deductible
Only the value of the donated services is deductible
Only the commuting costs are deductible as a charitable gift

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The value of a taxpayer's donated personal services is never a deductible charitable contribution, and ordinary commuting between home and a regular workplace is a nondeductible personal expense. Why the others are wrong: **A** neither item is deductible; **C** donated services have no deductible value (though certain out-of-pocket costs of volunteering may qualify); **D** commuting is personal, not a charitable gift.

questions.stem: Which two requirements must generally be met for an individual to claim the Lifetime Learning Credit for 2025 (ignoring income phase-outs)? (Select two.)

options.text: The expenses must be qualified tuition and related expenses paid to an eligible educational institution
The student must be enrolled at least half-time in a degree program
The credit may be claimed for the student, spouse, or a dependent the taxpayer claims
The credit is limited to the student's first four years of postsecondary education

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, C):** The Lifetime Learning Credit requires qualified tuition and related expenses paid to an eligible institution, and it may be claimed for the taxpayer, the taxpayer's spouse, or a claimed dependent. Why the others are wrong: **B** the LLC does not require half-time enrollment or a degree program—even a single course to improve job skills can qualify; **D** the four-year limit and the degree/half-time rules apply to the American Opportunity Credit, not the Lifetime Learning Credit.

questions.stem: A U.S. citizen dies in 2025 leaving a gross estate. Which two statements about the federal estate tax are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: An unlimited marital deduction generally applies to property passing outright to a surviving spouse who is a U.S. citizen
The estate may claim a unified credit that shelters transfers up to the applicable exclusion amount before any tax is due
The estate tax applies to every estate regardless of size, with no exclusion
Property left to a surviving spouse is always fully taxable in the decedent's estate

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** A decedent's estate generally gets an unlimited marital deduction for qualifying property passing to a U.S.-citizen surviving spouse, and a unified credit shelters transfers up to the applicable exclusion amount before estate tax applies. Why the others are wrong: **C** only estates exceeding the large applicable exclusion amount owe estate tax, so it does not apply to every estate; **D** the marital deduction generally makes qualifying transfers to a surviving spouse nontaxable, contradicting 'always fully taxable.'

questions.stem: Owners forming a new business want limited liability for all members but also want the entity's income to pass through to the owners by default without an entity-level income tax and without a corporate election. Which entity best fits these goals?

options.text: A C corporation
A general partnership
A sole proprietorship
A multi-member limited liability company (LLC) treated by default as a partnership

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A multi-member LLC gives all members limited liability and, by default under the check-the-box rules, is taxed as a partnership—pass-through treatment with no entity-level income tax and no election required. Why the others are wrong: **A** a C corporation pays entity-level tax, defeating pass-through treatment; **B** a general partnership provides pass-through taxation but exposes the general partners to personal liability; **C** a sole proprietorship has a single owner and no liability shield.

questions.stem: A noncorporate taxpayer operates a profitable consulting business as a sole proprietorship and has taxable income below the applicable threshold. Which deduction may allow the owner to deduct a portion of the business's qualified income?

options.text: The dividends-received deduction
The foreign earned income exclusion
The qualified business income (QBI) deduction of up to 20% of qualified business income
The domestic production activities deduction, currently in effect

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The Section 199A qualified business income deduction generally lets eligible noncorporate owners of pass-through businesses (including sole proprietors) deduct up to 20% of qualified business income, subject to limits that fully apply only above the income thresholds. Why the others are wrong: **A** the dividends-received deduction is a C corporation provision; **B** the foreign earned income exclusion applies to foreign wages of individuals living abroad, not domestic business profits; **D** the domestic production activities deduction (former Section 199) was repealed.

questions.stem: An accrual-method business uses inventories of goods it sells. Which method must generally be used to determine the cost of goods sold for federal tax purposes?

options.text: Inventory may simply be ignored and all purchases deducted when paid
Only the units-of-production method is allowed for inventory
The business must value inventory and compute cost of goods sold using a consistent, permissible inventory method such as specific identification, FIFO, or LIFO
Inventory must always be valued at retail selling price

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A business that maintains inventory must account for it using a permissible, consistently applied method (such as specific identification, FIFO, or LIFO) and may value it at cost or, where allowed, at the lower of cost or market, to compute cost of goods sold. Why the others are wrong: **A** ignoring inventory and deducting purchases when paid distorts income and is not allowed for inventory-based businesses required to account for inventory; **B** units-of-production is a depreciation concept, not an inventory costing method; **D** inventory is generally valued at cost (or lower of cost or market), not retail selling price.

questions.stem: A C corporation distributes appreciated land (fair market value $80,000, adjusted basis $50,000) to a shareholder as a dividend. What is the federal tax consequence to the distributing corporation?

options.text: The corporation recognizes no gain because it merely distributed property
The corporation recognizes $30,000 of gain as if it had sold the land at fair market value
The corporation deducts the $80,000 distribution
The corporation recognizes a $50,000 loss

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** Under Section 311(b), a corporation that distributes appreciated property recognizes gain as if it had sold the property at fair market value, so it recognizes the $30,000 of built-in gain ($80,000 minus $50,000). Why the others are wrong: **A** appreciation triggers gain recognition at the corporate level on a non-liquidating distribution; **C** dividends are not deductible by the distributing corporation; **D** the land is appreciated, producing a gain, not a loss (and losses on such distributions are generally not recognized).

questions.stem: A calendar-year partnership did not request an extension. Under the general rule, what is the due date of its Form 1065 for the 2025 tax year?

options.text: April 15, 2026 (the same as an individual return)
Partnerships have no filing deadline
March 16, 2026 (the 15th day of the third month after the tax year ends falls on a Sunday, so the deadline is the next business day)

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** A partnership return (Form 1065) for a calendar-year partnership is generally due by the 15th day of the third month after year-end; for tax year 2025 that day (March 15, 2026) falls on a Sunday, so the deadline shifts to the next business day, March 16, 2026—and partners receive their Schedules K-1 before their own returns are due. Why the others are wrong: **A** April 15 is the individual (and C corporation) calendar-year deadline, not the partnership deadline; **B** July 15 is not the statutory partnership due date; **C** partnerships must file an annual information return by the due date.

questions.stem: A shareholder who owns 100% of an S corporation has a stock basis of $4,000 and is allocated a $10,000 ordinary loss for the year. The shareholder made no loans to the corporation and there is no debt basis. How much of the loss may the shareholder currently deduct?

options.text: The full $10,000, regardless of basis
$4,000, limited to the shareholder's basis, with the remaining $6,000 suspended and carried forward
$0, because S corporation losses are never deductible
$10,000 now, creating a negative basis of $6,000

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** An S corporation shareholder may deduct pass-through losses only to the extent of stock basis plus debt basis; with $4,000 of stock basis and no debt basis, only $4,000 is currently deductible and the remaining $6,000 is suspended and carried forward until basis is restored. Why the others are wrong: **A** the loss is limited by basis; **C** S corporation losses are deductible up to basis, not never; **D** basis cannot go below zero, so no negative basis is created.

questions.stem: A business sells real property used in its trade or business that it held for several years at a gain, and there is no depreciation recapture beyond straight-line. Under Section 1231, how is a net gain from such property generally characterized?

options.text: As ordinary income in all cases
As long-term capital gain (after applying the Section 1231 netting and any recapture of prior 1231 losses)
As tax-free because business real estate gains are exempt
As a short-term capital gain regardless of holding period

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** A net Section 1231 gain from the sale of depreciable property and real property used in a trade or business and held long-term is generally treated as long-term capital gain, subject to the five-year lookback recapturing prior net 1231 losses as ordinary income. Why the others are wrong: **A** a net 1231 gain is capital, not ordinary (apart from recapture); **C** business real estate gains are taxable, not exempt; **D** qualifying 1231 property is held long-term, so the gain is not short-term.

questions.stem: A C corporation makes $30,000 of cash charitable contributions in 2025. Its taxable income before the charitable deduction (and before certain other items) is $200,000. What is the general limit on a C corporation's deductible charitable contributions for the year?

options.text: 60% of taxable income, the same as the individual cash-gift limit
Corporations may not deduct charitable contributions at all
10% of taxable income computed with specified modifications, with excess carried forward up to five years
There is no limit; corporations may deduct unlimited charitable gifts

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** A C corporation's charitable contribution deduction is generally limited to 10% of its taxable income (computed with specified modifications), and contributions exceeding the limit carry forward for up to five years. Why the others are wrong: **A** the 60%-of-AGI limit applies to individual cash gifts to public charities, not to corporations; **B** corporations may deduct charitable contributions within the limit; **D** corporate charitable deductions are subject to the 10% ceiling, not unlimited.

questions.stem: A grantor creates a revocable living trust and retains the power to revoke it and control the assets. During the grantor's life, how is the trust's income generally taxed for federal purposes?

options.text: The trust is a separate taxpayer that pays tax at compressed trust rates
Under the grantor trust rules, the income is taxed directly to the grantor on the grantor's own return
The income is entirely tax-free while the grantor is alive
The beneficiaries are taxed even though no distributions are made

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** When a grantor retains powers such as the power to revoke, the grantor trust rules treat the grantor as the owner, so the trust's income, deductions, and credits are reported directly on the grantor's individual return rather than on a separate trust return. Why the others are wrong: **A** a grantor trust is generally not taxed as a separate entity at trust rates; **C** the income is taxable—to the grantor; **D** beneficiaries are taxed on distributions of a non-grantor trust's income, which is not the situation for a revocable grantor trust.

questions.stem: A business owner uses a personal vehicle partly for business and wants the simplest method to deduct vehicle costs without tracking actual expenses like gas and repairs. Which method generally allows this?

options.text: The standard mileage rate method, multiplying business miles by the IRS rate
Deducting the full purchase price of the car each year
Deducting 100% of all personal and business driving costs
Deducting commuting miles between home and the regular office

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The standard mileage rate method lets a taxpayer deduct business vehicle use by multiplying qualifying business miles by the IRS standard rate, avoiding the need to track actual operating costs. Why the others are wrong: **B** the car's cost is recovered through depreciation limits, not fully expensed each year under this method; **C** only the business-use portion is deductible, not personal driving; **D** ordinary commuting between home and a regular workplace is nondeductible personal mileage.

questions.stem: Which two characteristics distinguish a C corporation from an S corporation for federal income tax purposes? (Select two.)

options.text: Only a C corporation may issue stock to its owners
An S corporation must always pay tax on its income twice
A C corporation pays income tax at the entity level, whereas an S corporation generally does not
A C corporation has no statutory limit on the number or type of shareholders, whereas an S corporation does

questions.explanation: **Correct (C, D):** A C corporation is a separate taxpayer that pays entity-level income tax and may have unlimited shareholders of any type, while an S corporation is generally a pass-through limited to 100 eligible shareholders and one class of stock. Why the others are wrong: **A** both C and S corporations issue stock to shareholders; **B** S corporation income is generally taxed once at the shareholder level, not twice—double taxation is the C corporation feature.

questions.stem: Which two statements correctly describe the federal tax treatment of fringe benefits a partnership provides to a partner versus an S corporation provides to a more-than-2% shareholder-employee? (Select two.)

options.text: A partner who receives guaranteed payments for services reports them as ordinary income, and they are deductible by the partnership
Health insurance premiums paid for a more-than-2% S corporation shareholder-employee are generally included in that shareholder's W-2 wages
Partners are treated as common-law employees of their own partnership for fringe benefit purposes
A more-than-2% S corporation shareholder is fully exempt from reporting any employer-provided benefits

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** Guaranteed payments to a partner for services are ordinary income to the partner and deductible by the partnership, and health insurance premiums for a more-than-2% S corporation shareholder-employee are generally added to that shareholder's W-2 wages (with a possible offsetting self-employed health insurance deduction). Why the others are wrong: **C** partners are not employees of their own partnership, so many tax-favored employee fringe benefits do not apply to them; **D** a more-than-2% shareholder is not exempt—certain benefits are taxable and reportable to that shareholder.

questions.stem: Order the following steps a sole proprietor follows to arrive at the income that flows to the individual return, from earliest to latest.

options.text: Total the business's gross receipts and sales for the year
Subtract cost of goods sold to determine gross profit
Deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses to compute net profit on Schedule C
Carry the Schedule C net profit to Form 1040 and compute self-employment tax on it

questions.explanation: The Schedule C computation flows in this order: first total the business's gross receipts and sales (A); then subtract cost of goods sold to arrive at gross profit (B); next deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses to reach net profit (C); and finally carry that net profit to Form 1040, where it is included in income and used to compute self-employment tax (D). The sequence matters because each subtotal feeds the next, and self-employment tax is figured on the net profit only after expenses are subtracted.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to authorize an enrolled agent only to receive and inspect confidential tax information from the IRS, but not to advocate or represent the taxpayer in an examination. Which form accomplishes exactly this?

options.text: Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization
Form 2848, Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative
Form 911, Request for Taxpayer Advocate Service Assistance
Form 1040-X, Amended U.S. Individual Income Tax Return

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Form 8821 is a tax information authorization that lets a designee receive and inspect a taxpayer's confidential tax information, but it does not authorize the designee to represent or advocate for the taxpayer. Why the others are wrong: **B** Form 2848 grants representation authority, which is more than the taxpayer wants here; **C** Form 911 requests Taxpayer Advocate Service help, not an information authorization; **D** Form 1040-X amends a return and has nothing to do with authorizing information disclosure.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent represents a taxpayer in an examination of the 2022 individual return, which the taxpayer filed on time on April 15, 2023, with no fraud or substantial omission. Under the general rule, by when must the IRS ordinarily assess additional tax?

options.text: Within three years after the return was filed (generally by April 15, 2026)
Within one year after the return was filed
There is no time limit on assessment for an accurate return
Within ten years after the return was filed

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The general statute of limitations on assessment is three years from the later of the due date or the date the return was filed, so for a timely 2022 return the IRS ordinarily must assess by about April 15, 2026. Why the others are wrong: **B** the general assessment period is three years, not one; **C** a limitations period does apply absent fraud or a substantial (over-25%) omission or no return; **D** the ten-year period is the collection statute that runs after assessment, not the assessment limitations period.

questions.stem: After an Appeals conference fails to resolve a dispute and the taxpayer wants to litigate but prefers a forum where the case is heard by a jury, which court is generally available if the taxpayer first pays the tax and sues for a refund?

options.text: The U.S. Tax Court
A U.S. district court
The IRS Independent Office of Appeals
The Office of Professional Responsibility

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** To litigate in a U.S. district court, the taxpayer must first pay the disputed tax and file a refund suit; the district court is the forum where a jury trial is generally available in a federal tax refund case. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Tax Court hears cases without prepayment but does not provide jury trials; **C** Appeals is an administrative body, not a court; **D** the Office of Professional Responsibility disciplines practitioners and does not adjudicate tax refund suits.

questions.stem: The IRS asserts the trust fund recovery penalty against an individual. To whom does this penalty generally apply, and what does it cover?

options.text: Any shareholder of a corporation, covering all corporate income taxes
A responsible person who willfully failed to collect or pay over withheld income and employment taxes, equal to the unpaid trust fund portion
Only the IRS examiner who audited the return
Every employee of a business, regardless of authority

questions.explanation: **Correct (B):** The trust fund recovery penalty under Section 6672 applies to a responsible person who willfully fails to collect, account for, or pay over withheld income and employment (trust fund) taxes, and equals 100% of the unpaid trust fund amount. Why the others are wrong: **A** it targets responsible persons for trust fund taxes, not all shareholders for corporate income tax; **C** the penalty falls on the responsible person in the business, not the IRS examiner; **D** it applies only to those with responsibility and willfulness, not every employee.

questions.stem: A taxpayer owes a balance but, after paying necessary living expenses, has no ability to make any payment, and collection would create economic hardship. Which IRS status may temporarily suspend active collection?

options.text: Placing the account in currently not collectible (CNC) status
Filing a Tax Court petition
Requesting a private letter ruling
Submitting a Form W-4 adjustment

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** When a taxpayer cannot pay anything without creating economic hardship, the IRS may report the account currently not collectible, temporarily pausing active collection (though interest continues and the balance remains due). Why the others are wrong: **B** a Tax Court petition disputes a deficiency, not a hardship collection pause; **C** a private letter ruling addresses prospective tax treatment, not collection hardship; **D** a Form W-4 adjusts wage withholding and does not suspend collection of an existing balance.

questions.stem: Which two statements about claiming a refund of overpaid federal income tax are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: There is no deadline for filing a refund claim
A refund claim generally must be filed within three years from the date the return was filed or two years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later
A refund is claimed by filing Form 2848
An individual amends a previously filed return to claim a refund using Form 1040-X

questions.explanation: **Correct (B, D):** A claim for refund generally must be filed within three years from filing the return or two years from paying the tax, whichever is later, and an individual claims a refund on a previously filed return by filing Form 1040-X. Why the others are wrong: **A** a refund claim is subject to the limitations period, so there is a deadline; **C** Form 2848 grants a power of attorney and does not itself claim a refund.

questions.stem: Under Circular 230, when a client asks for written advice on a federal tax matter, what standard must the practitioner generally follow?

options.text: Base the advice on reasonable factual and legal assumptions, consider all relevant facts the practitioner knows or reasonably should know, and not rely on unreasonable representations
Assume the most favorable outcome for the client regardless of the facts
Take into account the likelihood the position will be audited when evaluating the merits
Provide only oral advice, because written advice is prohibited

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Circular 230 section 10.37 requires written advice to be based on reasonable factual and legal assumptions, to consider all facts the practitioner knows or reasonably should know, and not to rely on unreasonable representations or assumptions. Why the others are wrong: **B** the practitioner cannot simply assume a favorable result; competent analysis is required; **C** the practitioner may not base the advice on the chance that the position will not be audited; **D** written tax advice is permitted and governed by the standard, not prohibited.

questions.stem: An enrolled agent must complete continuing education and renew the enrollment to remain in active status. Which office administers enrollment and the continuing education requirements for enrolled agents?

options.text: The Securities and Exchange Commission
The U.S. Tax Court
The IRS Return Preparer Office (which administers PTINs and enrolled agent enrollment)
The Financial Accounting Standards Board

questions.explanation: **Correct (C):** The IRS Return Preparer Office administers PTINs and the enrolled agent program, including enrollment, renewal, and continuing education tracking, while the Office of Professional Responsibility handles disciplinary matters under Circular 230. Why the others are wrong: **A** the SEC regulates securities markets, not enrolled agents; **B** the Tax Court adjudicates tax disputes and admits its own practitioners, but does not administer EA enrollment; **D** the FASB sets financial accounting standards and has no role in EA enrollment.

questions.stem: A taxpayer substantially understates income tax on a return, and the understatement is large relative to the correct tax. Absent reasonable cause, which accuracy-related penalty most directly applies to the taxpayer?

options.text: A 20% accuracy-related penalty on the portion of the underpayment attributable to the substantial understatement (or to negligence)
A 100% penalty equal to the entire tax
No penalty, because only preparers can be penalized
A 75% civil fraud penalty applies automatically to any understatement

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** The Section 6662 accuracy-related penalty is generally 20% of the underpayment attributable to a substantial understatement of income tax or to negligence or disregard of rules, absent reasonable cause and good faith. Why the others are wrong: **B** there is no general 100%-of-tax accuracy penalty; **C** taxpayers themselves face accuracy-related penalties, not just preparers; **D** the 75% civil fraud penalty applies only where fraud is proven, not automatically to every understatement.

questions.stem: An electronic return originator (ERO) e-files an individual return for a client. Which document does the taxpayer generally sign to authorize the ERO to electronically transmit the return and, if applicable, a direct debit?

options.text: Form 8879, IRS e-file Signature Authorization
Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement
Form SS-4, Application for Employer Identification Number
Form 4506-T, Request for Transcript of Tax Return

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Form 8879 is the e-file signature authorization a taxpayer signs to let the ERO enter or generate the taxpayer's PIN and transmit the e-filed return (and authorize any electronic funds withdrawal). Why the others are wrong: **B** Form W-2 reports wages and is not a signature authorization; **C** Form SS-4 requests an EIN; **D** Form 4506-T requests a tax transcript, not e-file authorization.

questions.stem: Under Section 7216, a tax return preparer wants to use a client's return information to solicit the client for a separate financial product. What is generally required before the preparer may do so?

options.text: The preparer must obtain the taxpayer's prior, knowing, written consent that meets the regulatory requirements
Nothing; preparers may freely use client return information for any marketing purpose
Only the IRS's approval, not the client's
A verbal acknowledgment from the client is always sufficient

questions.explanation: **Correct (A):** Section 7216 and its regulations generally prohibit a preparer from using or disclosing a client's tax return information for purposes such as marketing unrelated products unless the taxpayer gives prior, knowing, written consent that satisfies the specific format and content rules. Why the others are wrong: **B** unrestricted use is exactly what the rule forbids; **C** it is the taxpayer's consent that is required, not IRS approval; **D** the consent must generally be written and meet regulatory requirements, so a mere verbal okay is insufficient.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties on an individual income tax return are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: The failure-to-file penalty generally accrues at a higher monthly rate than the failure-to-pay penalty
Either penalty may be abated if the taxpayer shows reasonable cause and not willful neglect
Neither penalty can ever be removed once it has been assessed
The failure-to-pay penalty is a flat one-time 50% charge

questions.explanation: **Correct (A, B):** The failure-to-file penalty accrues at a higher monthly rate than the failure-to-pay penalty, and both penalties may be abated where the taxpayer demonstrates reasonable cause and the absence of willful neglect. Why the others are wrong: **C** the penalties can be abated for reasonable cause (and may qualify for first-time abatement), so they are not permanently fixed once assessed; **D** the failure-to-pay penalty accrues monthly up to a maximum, not as a one-time 50% charge.

questions.stem: A taxpayer wants to petition the U.S. Tax Court to dispute a deficiency, and the amount in dispute is modest. The taxpayer prefers a simpler, more informal proceeding even though the decision cannot be appealed. Which option fits?

options.text: Demand a jury trial in the Tax Court
Bypass the Tax Court and appeal directly to the Supreme Court
Pay the tax first and then petition the Tax Court for a refund
Elect the Tax Court small tax case (S case) procedure for disputes at or below the dollar limit

questions.explanation: **Correct (D):** The Tax Court's small tax case (S case) procedure offers a simpler, more informal process for disputes that do not exceed the statutory dollar limit, but the decision is final and cannot be appealed. Why the others are wrong: **A** the Tax Court does not conduct jury trials; **B** a litigant cannot leapfrog directly to the Supreme Court; **C** the Tax Court is a prepayment forum—paying first and suing for a refund describes district court or the Court of Federal Claims, not the Tax Court.

flashcards.back: A qualifying child must meet relationship, age (under 19, or under 24 if a full-time student, or any age if permanently disabled), residency, support, and joint-return tests. A qualifying relative has no age test but must meet a gross-income limit and be supported more than half by the taxpayer.

Total (gross) income minus above-the-line adjustments (e.g., one-half of self-employment tax, deductible IRA contributions, student loan interest). AGI is the base for many phase-outs and limits, and you subtract the standard or itemized deduction from AGI to reach taxable income.

A taxpayer who owned and used a home as a principal residence for at least 2 of the last 5 years may exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 if married filing jointly and both meet the use test). Generally usable only once every two years.

Holding period of one year or less is short-term (taxed at ordinary rates); more than one year is long-term (taxed at preferential 0%/15%/20% rates). Gains and losses are netted within each class, then short-term and long-term results are netted against each other.

Avoid the underpayment penalty by paying the smaller of 90% of the current year's tax or 100% of the prior year's tax (110% if prior-year AGI exceeded $150,000) through withholding and timely estimates.

Partnerships and S corporations pass income through to owners, who pay tax on their distributive share whether or not it is distributed; the entity pays no income tax. A C corporation pays entity-level tax, and dividends are taxed again to shareholders (double taxation).

Must be a domestic corporation with no more than 100 shareholders, only one class of stock, and only eligible shareholders (generally U.S. citizens/residents, certain trusts and estates—no partnerships, corporations, or nonresident aliens). Elect on Form 2553.

On the sale of depreciable personal property at a gain, gain is recaptured as ordinary income up to the total depreciation previously claimed; any remaining gain is generally Section 1231 (capital) gain.

Increase outside basis for contributions, share of income/gains, and share of partnership liabilities. Decrease it for distributions, share of losses, nondeductible expenses, and decreases in liability share. Basis cannot go below zero.

Form 2848 (Power of Attorney) authorizes an eligible representative to act and advocate for the taxpayer before the IRS. Form 8821 (Tax Information Authorization) only permits the IRS to disclose information to a designee—no representation.

An IRS notice asserting a deficiency that gives the taxpayer 90 days (150 if addressed outside the U.S.) to petition the U.S. Tax Court without first paying the tax. Missing the deadline allows the IRS to assess and bill the tax.

Circular 230 sets the rules governing practice before the IRS. The Office of Professional Responsibility enforces it and can censure, suspend, disbar, or monetarily penalize practitioners. Enrolled agents have unlimited practice rights before the IRS.
